newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

SUGAR: World market for September 11 - White sugar futures fell in heavy trading as traders continued to sell spot-October ahead of the contract's expiry on Friday. October ended $3.50 lower at $345.20 a tonne while December lost $3.50 to close at $345.20.

In New York raw sugar futures ended lower on commission-house selling. Speculators continued to roll long positions into March ahead of the October contract's expiry at the end of the month. October lost 9 points to close at 11.96 cents/lb while March shed 7 points to close at 11.66 cents/lb. The back months ended unchanged to 4 points lower. FUNDAMENTALS

RUSSIA/UKRAINE - Russia plans to levy a value-added tax of 10 per cent on all raw and refined sugar imports from the Ukraine beginning October 1. Last month a Russian government commission recommended that white sugar imports from the CIS (mainly the Ukraine) should be kept at 1.5 million tonnes annually for 1996 and 1997.

The Ukrainians said that the tax is discriminatory and would have a disastrous effect on the Ukrainian sugar industry. The problem for the Ukrainians is that Russia and some other ex-Soviet republics are the only markets for their sugar as it is not competitive internationally.

For 1996 such a limit would be no problem for the Ukraine as production in 1995/96 is forecast to fall to 2.8 million tonnes in raw value terms down from 3.8 million tonnes the previous year, which would leave an exportable surplus of a little more than one million tonnes. However, if production should recover, the Ukraine would face a significant surplus problem. The only way out would be a downsizing of the Ukrainian sugar industry.

RUSSIA - By September 9, the harvested sugar beet area reached 22,000 ha (about 2.1 per cent of total plantings), compared with 52,500 ha at the same date last year. Harvesting has made progress in the North Caucasus while in the Central Chernozem, Povolzhsk and Central it has just begun. Harvesting has not yet commenced in the Urals, West Siberia and Volgo- Vyatsk.

In all regions, harvesting operations are lagging behind those of last year. Average yields so far are 20.2 tonnes per ha, roughly equal to that of last year. At this stage, however, such a comparison is not quite correct because the North Caucasus accounts for the bulk of harvested area. As a result, average yields reflect virtually yields achieved from the area harvested in one region so far.

The general impression is that yields will be lower than last season with reductions from 8 per cent (the North Caucasus) to 17 per cent (Central Chernozem). Average sugar beet yields are expected to be 15.5 to 16.3 tonnes per ha or around 11 per cent down on last year.

The total beet crop is now expected to reach 16- 17.5 million tonnes or some 12 per cent less than last year. This would be the second-lowest output for the last 40 years after 1993. However, all forecasts at this stage are tentative and weather conditions will still have a crucial role to play.

GREECE - The latest beet test results of August 31 show a satisfactory increase in beet weight and sugar content although the overall results are still far from being good. Beet weight on August 31, 1996 amounted to 73.46 tonnes per ha, down from 80.62 tonnes in 1995 and below the average (91/95) of 78.24 tonnes.

Sugar content reached 13.74 per cent, up from 13.38 per cent in 1995 and the average of 13.60 per cent. This resulted in a theoretical sugar weight per ha of 10.00 tonnes, down on last year's 10.75 tonnes but up on the five-year average of 10.66 tonnes. The latest results suggest that Greece will have a lower crop than in 1995 when it produced 312,000 tonnes, raw value.

SWITZERLAND - The latest beet test results for Switzerland (September 10) show a below average increase in beet weight whereas sugar content is developping very favourably. Beet yields per ha amounted to 87.1 tonnes, sharply up from last year's 67.6 tonnes and also much improved on the average (1991/95) of 66.4 tonnes.

Sugar content was measured at 17.5 per cent, up from last year's 15.9 per cent and the average of 15.8 per cent. This resulted in a theoretical sugar yield per ha of 15.25 tonnes, almost 50 per cent up on 1995 (10.75 tonnes) and the average of 10.49 tonnes. Together with the higher area sown to beet, Switzerland can be expected to have an excellent crop this year.

UNITED KINGDOM - The latest beet test results of September 9 suggest that the beet crop is heading for a better result than last year. Root weight on September 9 reached 591 grams, up from 511 grams in 1995 and against the average (91/95) of 580 grams. Sugar content reached 16.11 per cent, down from 16.92 per cent in 1995 and below the five-year average of 17.37 per cent. Due to the high root weight, sugar per root now stands at 95.2 grams, up from 86.5 grams in 1995 but still somewhat below the average of 100.8 grams. British sugar continues to be confident that normal results will be achieved. TENDERS

The European Union awarded 93,500 tonnes of white sugar at a maximum refund of ECU 43.392 per 100 kg at its weekly tender on Wednesday. Cumulative awards so far made under the 1996/97 series of tenders for the period up to September 11 reached 183 750 tonnes, which compares to 475 500 tonnes last year.
